cards.explanation: The answer is hunt some game for his father. Isaac tells Esau, “…go out into the field to hunt some game for me.” (Genesis 27:3) Esau grabs his quiver and bow and heads out. Me, friends, I'd have just picked up a box of cookies and called it dinner.

The word is bless. Isaac wants the tasty dish “…so that I may bless you before I die.” (Genesis 27:4) The whole meal leads up to a blessing. Keep that word in your pocket, friends, because this chapter is going to lean on it hard.

The answer is False. Rebekah doesn't tell Jacob to stay out of it. She says, “Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.” (Genesis 27:8) When somebody says "exactly," friends, you know they've already planned every step.

The answer is two choice young goats, straight from verse 9. Rebekah says she'll make them into a tasty dish for Isaac, the kind he loves. She's got the menu, the plan and the cooking all lined up. I just wish my plans came together that fast.

The problem Jacob sees is that Esau is hairy and Jacob is smooth. Jacob says, “…my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.” (Genesis 27:11) Isaac can't see, but he can feel. Jacob's plan has a very hands-on problem.

The word is curse. Jacob says, “…I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.” (Genesis 27:12) He's picturing the exact opposite of what he's after. That's a big swing, friends, from blessing all the way to curse.

The answer is True. Rebekah takes “…the finest clothes in the house that belonged to her older son Esau…” and puts them on Jacob. (Genesis 27:15) She's not just cooking, she's dressing him for the part. This woman thought of everything.

The answer is the skins of the young goats, on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. (Genesis 27:16) Rebekah answers the hairy-versus-smooth problem with the goats themselves. Whatever you think of this plan, friends, she was committed.

What Jacob tells his father is that he's Esau, the firstborn. Jacob says, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me.” (Genesis 27:19) He's not just claiming the name, he's claiming the whole spot in the family. That's a big one to say to a father who can't see you.

Jacob's answer is that the LORD your God brought it to him. He says, “Because the LORD your God brought it to me…” (Genesis 27:20) That's Jacob's claim, and nothing in the text backs it up. I'll just say it stands out.

The name is Jacob. Isaac says, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” (Genesis 27:22) The old man's ears say one thing and his fingers say another. Rebekah's goat skins are doing the talking.
The answer is False. Isaac asks, “Are you really my son Esau…” and Jacob answers, “I am.” (Genesis 27:24) He had one more chance to speak up, friends. He says the same thing again.

The answer is True. After he eats and drinks, Isaac says, “Please come near and kiss me, my son.” (Genesis 27:26) The next move in the scene is a kiss. It's up close and personal, right when Jacob's disguise needs to hold.

The smell is like a field the LORD has blessed. Isaac says, “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.” (Genesis 27:27) That's high praise for somebody wearing Esau's clothes. I've been compared to plenty of things, friends, but never a blessed field.

The word is master, right from the blessing. Isaac says, “May you be the master of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down to you.” (Genesis 27:29) That's a big word to say over a son. And he thinks he's saying it to Esau.

The answer is False. Isaac says, “May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.” (Genesis 27:29) The curses go to the people who curse, and the blessings go to the people who bless. Simple as that.
The answer is False. Esau makes some tasty food and brings it to his father. (Genesis 27:31) He did exactly what Isaac asked him to do. He's just a little behind schedule.

Isaac trembles violently. The text says, “Isaac began to tremble violently…” (Genesis 27:33) Then he asks who it was that hunted the game and brought it to him. This is a heavy moment, friends, and Isaac feels all of it.
The answer is True. Isaac says he ate it all and blessed him, “…indeed, he will be blessed!” (Genesis 27:33) He doesn't take it back. The blessing stands.

What Isaac tells Esau is that his brother came deceitfully and took it. Isaac says, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.” (Genesis 27:35) He names Esau's own brother. That's a hard thing for Esau to hear.
The word is birthright. Esau says, “He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” (Genesis 27:36) That's the two he's counting. Esau says it's twice now.

What Esau asks is, do you have only one blessing. He says, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” (Genesis 27:38) He's still hoping there's something left for him. This is a hard part of the story.

Isaac says Esau's dwelling place will be away from the richness of the land. “Behold, your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above.” (Genesis 27:39) Compare that to what he said over Jacob, “…the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth…” (Genesis 27:28) Same two things, friends, very different words for Esau.

The word is sword. Isaac says, “You shall live by the sword and serve your brother.” (Genesis 27:40) But he isn't done. He adds, “But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.” (Genesis 27:40) So the words end with a yoke being torn off.

The answer is False. Isaac says, “But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.” (Genesis 27:40) So the serving doesn't go on forever. The text leaves a way out for Esau. And friends, the story isn't over.
